cd /hutian/wiki/w; cat > Brief.md <<'EOF'
# Brief — idea of the study (revision 2, after idea-review round 1)

## Question
With network interference, how accurate is the regression-based GATE estimator (fit outcome on functions of the assignment vector — own treatment, treated-neighbour fraction/count, higher-order terms — then predict at all-treated and all-control and difference; Chin 2019, Han & Ugander 2023)? What determines its error, and under which interference mechanisms, networks and designs does it hold, fail, or lose to the biased difference in means?

## Thesis (the claim the paper is built around)
The regression GATE estimator is limited by **extrapolation from the observed exposure distribution to the global-treatment and global-control corners**, and the two parts of its error — variance and bias — have *different* drivers that move in opposite directions with degree. A data-computable two-part diagnostic separates them and tells an experimenter when to trust the estimate, when a flexible learner cannot rescue it, and when the biased DM is the better choice. The extrapolation viewpoint itself is not new (Chin 2019 shows the feature distributions at global treatment/control differ from the observed one and invokes off-policy evaluation, qualitatively); the claimed contribution is the quantified, tested account, its interaction with the design, and the regime map including where regression loses.

### Notation
Features φ_i(z) (own z_i; treated-neighbour fraction f_i; optional count, 2-hop, interaction terms). τ̂ = Δxᵀβ̂ with Δx = mean_i[φ_i(1) − φ_i(0)] (the intercept cancels). Corner offsets: raw exposure distances of the corners from the observed exposure distribution, (1−p) for all-treated and p for all-control (fraction feature; mechanism-specific for count/2-hop).

### Predictions (fixed now; each falsifiable)
**Variance part.**
- *Leverage* L = Δxᵀ Σ̂_φ⁻¹ Δx, Σ̂_φ the empirical covariance of the feature rows under the observed assignment (pooled primary; the per-unit average of per-unit leverage is reported as variant for heterogeneous degree). For the fraction feature, L ≈ (1+d·1)/(p(1−p)) i.e. ∝ d/(p(1−p)); minimal at p = ½.
- P1. Where residuals are independent with variance σ², Var(τ̂) ≈ σ² L / n (OLS leverage; textbook, stated as the baseline, not the finding). The test is the *departure*: fit log-RMSE on log n, log d, log p(1−p) with CIs, on graphs where the iid formula is expected to hold (ER/SBM, Bernoulli) and where not (BA hubs, cluster designs, degree-correlated baselines, 2-hop features with shared neighbours); report where σ²L/n over- or under-states the realised variance and by what factor (an effective-n). Noise model fixed: iid Gaussian ε with σ a multiple of the SD of the noise-free outcome ({0.25,0.5,1}), plus unit baselines a_i that are iid or degree/community-correlated; with σ=0 and correct spec the error is exactly 0 and such cells serve only as a sanity check.
**Bias part.**
- P2. For a response g(f) curved in exposure and a linear fit tangent near p, spillover bias ≈ −½g''(1−2p) to second order (zero at p = ½), plus a third-order term −(1/6)g'''[(1−p)³+p³]; it depends on *raw* distance × curvature and **not** on d (large d only narrows the observed support, so the bias neither grows nor shrinks with d for the fraction feature). For threshold/complex-contagion responses with the threshold outside the observed support the linear fit sees no spillover and bias is the whole jump, independent of d; at small d the support is wide enough to straddle the threshold and bias is smaller. For count-type features and 2-hop mechanisms each mechanism's predicted scaling is derived and written in the analysis plan before running. Flexible learners do not remove this bias (trees extrapolate flat, polynomials explode); they may win in-sample prediction yet not GATE error.

Brief revised (wiki `Brief`, revision 2) and `prior_work.md`/`.bib` extended (main). The review was right on the core point and changed the claim.

- **1 (D conflated two errors):** corrected. The variance driver is now the difference-leverage L = ΔxᵀΣ⁻¹Δx (≈(1+d)/(p(1−p)) for own z + neighbour fraction), the bias driver is raw corner distance × curvature, with the second/third-order expansion (zero at p=½, minimiser shifts for g'''≠0) and a d-independence prediction for the fraction feature. P5 is now two-part (L; specification-disagreement S + corner distance outside observed support). Net prediction written: d raises variance, leaves bias roughly constant.
- **2 (P1 textbook):** kept as the reference identity; the test is departure (exponent fits with CIs, BA/cluster/degree-correlated cases, effective-n factor). Noise model fixed. Pooled L is primary, per-unit average a reported variant.
- **3 (P5 trivial):** benchmarks, within-cell and held-out-by-mechanism/family protocol, and a numeric acceptance rule fixed before running; the γ circularity handled (estimated and oracle share both reported).
- **4, 6 (fair terms, oracle):** three information tiers (generic / data-adaptive / oracle with parameters known vs fitted); comparisons only inside a tier. Thiyageswaran et al. 2024 and Shirani & Bayati 2024 added (abstracts read).
- **5, 7:** calibration to a common τ and spillover share s, errors normalised by fixed τ; p grid extended to {0.75, 0.9}.
- **8–11:** cluster resolution rule/sweep, modularity-based cluster quality, cluster bootstrap; fixed model-selection protocol, GNN on a subset; nested variance sources; core factorial + one-factor slices with the rest exploratory, to be mapped to cells with `story-repo`.
- **Positioning:** I read the relevant parts of Chin, Han–Ugander and Gao–Ding. Chin already shows the feature-distribution mismatch (Fig. 2) and invokes off-policy evaluation, qualitatively, so the claim is now the quantified, tested account, stated "within the literature checked", with the overlap literature (Crump et al., D'Amour et al.) cited. Headline emphasis moved to the design × estimator × regime map and where regression loses.
EOF

I revised the `Brief` (revision 2) after the idea review and extended `prior_work.md` and `prior_work.bib`. I replied on `idea-repo`#3 and closed it. The review was right that the central claim had a formulation error. Nothing here has been run yet; all the predictions are still untested.

- **Two drivers, not one:**
  - **Variance:** it is driven by the difference-leverage `L = ΔxᵀΣ⁻¹Δx`, which is about (1+d)/(p(1−p)) for own treatment plus neighbour fraction.
  - **Bias:** from a curved response it is driven by raw corner distance times curvature, and it does not grow with degree for the fraction feature.
  - **Net prediction:** higher degree raises variance but leaves bias roughly constant.
- **Diagnostic:** it is now two-part, leverage plus a specification-disagreement term. It must beat trivial predictors such as mean degree, p(1−p) and the bootstrap SE. It is tested within a cell and on held-out mechanisms and graph families. A numeric acceptance rule is fixed before any run.
- **Fair comparisons:** baselines are compared only within three information tiers (generic, data-adaptive, oracle). Two competitors were added: data-adaptive exposure thresholds for HT (Thiyageswaran et al. 2024) and causal message-passing (Shirani & Bayati 2024). I read only their abstracts.
- **Design fixes:**
  - Mechanisms are calibrated to a common τ and spillover share.
  - The p grid now includes 0.75 and 0.9.
  - Cluster resolution is swept or fixed by a rule.
  - Cluster designs use a cluster bootstrap.
  - The compute plan is a core factorial plus one-factor-at-a-time slices, with the rest labelled exploratory.
- **Novelty:** I read the relevant parts of Chin, Han–Ugander and Gao–Ding. Chin (2019) already shows that the feature distributions at global treatment/control differ from the observed one, and draws the off-policy-evaluation analogy. So extrapolation as a viewpoint is not new. The claim is now the quantified, tested account, stated "within the literature checked", and the headline moves to the design × estimator × regime map and where regression loses.

I still owe the commitment issue `idea-repo`#2, which stays open until the work is delivered.
